Dr. James Naismith, the inventor of basketball, practicing with his wife. University of Kansas. 1928.

James Naismith (November 6, 1861 – November 28, 1939) was a Canadian-American physical educator and physician. He invented the sport of basketball in 1891. He wrote the original basketball rulebook, founded the University of Kansas basketball program, and lived to see basketball adopted as as an official event at the 1936 Summer Olympics in Berlin.

While working at the Springfield YMCA in Massachusetts, Naismith struggled with a rowdy class which was confined to indoor games throughout the New England winter. Under orders from the head of Springfield YMCA Physical Education, Naismith was given 14 days to create an indoor game that would provide an "athletic distraction". The first game of "Basket Ball" was played in December 1891. In a handwritten report, Naismith described the circumstances of the inaugural match; in contrast to modern basketball, the players played nine versus nine, handled a soccer ball, not a basketball, and instead of shooting at two hoops, the goals were a pair of peach baskets. By 1893, basketball was introduced internationally by the YMCA. By 1900, there were enough college teams in the East of the U.S. that the first intercollegiate competitions could be played.
